steps.title: Why start with OrderDetails?
steps.change: Finance wants sold units to add back to the original sales. One row here represents a sale line. Order `100` spans three lines, each with its own product and quantity.

steps.title: Why LEFT JOIN to Products?
steps.change: 🟩 `Products` comes second because it supplies the price and the category reference for each 🟦 sale line. The `LEFT JOIN` keeps line 5 and its four units even though product ID `999` has no match. The two product ID columns below distinguish the ID recorded on the order from the product actually found.
steps.added_sql:
SELECT od.OrderDetailID, od.OrderID, od.ProductID AS ordered_product_id, od.Quantity,
       p.ProductID AS matched_product_id, p.CategoryID AS product_category_id, p.Sale_Price
FROM OrderDetails AS od
LEFT JOIN Products AS p
    ON od.ProductID = p.ProductID
ORDER BY od.OrderDetailID;
steps.sql:
SELECT od.OrderDetailID, od.OrderID, od.ProductID AS ordered_product_id, od.Quantity,
       p.ProductID AS matched_product_id, p.CategoryID AS product_category_id, p.Sale_Price
FROM OrderDetails AS od
LEFT JOIN Products AS p
    ON od.ProductID = p.ProductID
ORDER BY od.OrderDetailID;

steps.title: Why FULL OUTER JOIN to Category?
steps.change: The 🟩 `Products.CategoryID` obtained in step 2 supplies the key to add 🟥 `Category` third. The `FULL OUTER JOIN` preserves both an unmatched sale and a catalogue category with no matching sales, such as Stationery. Follow the last three rows. They show a product with a broken category reference, a sale with no product match, and a category with no sales.
steps.added_sql:
SELECT od.OrderDetailID, od.OrderID, od.ProductID AS ordered_product_id, od.Quantity,
       p.ProductID AS matched_product_id, p.CategoryID AS product_category_id, p.Sale_Price,
       c.CategoryID, c.CategoryName
FROM OrderDetails AS od
LEFT JOIN Products AS p
    ON od.ProductID = p.ProductID
FULL OUTER JOIN Category AS c
    ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID
ORDER BY od.OrderDetailID NULLS LAST;
steps.sql:
SELECT od.OrderDetailID, od.OrderID, od.ProductID AS ordered_product_id, od.Quantity,
       p.ProductID AS matched_product_id, p.CategoryID AS product_category_id, p.Sale_Price,
       c.CategoryID, c.CategoryName
FROM OrderDetails AS od
LEFT JOIN Products AS p
    ON od.ProductID = p.ProductID
FULL OUTER JOIN Category AS c
    ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID
ORDER BY od.OrderDetailID NULLS LAST;

steps.title: Why label missing matches before grouping?
steps.change: Use the catalogue name whenever the category exists. For a missing category, check the product lookup. A matched product earns `Unmapped`, and a missing product earns `Unknown product`. Stationery still has a category ID and retains its own name.
steps.added_sql:
SELECT od.OrderDetailID, c.CategoryID,
    CASE
        WHEN c.CategoryID IS NULL AND p.ProductID IS NULL
            THEN 'Unknown product'
        WHEN c.CategoryID IS NULL AND p.ProductID IS NOT NULL
            THEN 'Unmapped'
        WHEN c.CategoryID IS NOT NULL
            THEN c.CategoryName
    END AS category_name
steps.sql:
SELECT od.OrderDetailID, od.OrderID, od.Quantity, p.Sale_Price, c.CategoryID,
    CASE
        WHEN c.CategoryID IS NULL AND p.ProductID IS NULL
            THEN 'Unknown product'
        WHEN c.CategoryID IS NULL AND p.ProductID IS NOT NULL
            THEN 'Unmapped'
        WHEN c.CategoryID IS NOT NULL
            THEN c.CategoryName
    END AS category_name
FROM OrderDetails AS od
LEFT JOIN Products AS p
    ON od.ProductID = p.ProductID
FULL OUTER JOIN Category AS c
    ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID
ORDER BY od.OrderDetailID NULLS LAST;

steps.title: Why multiply price by quantity on each line?
steps.change: Drinks has two different prices within order `100`. Pair each price with its own line’s quantity while those values are still on the same row.
steps.sql:
SELECT od.OrderDetailID, od.OrderID, od.Quantity, p.Sale_Price, c.CategoryID,
    CASE
        WHEN c.CategoryID IS NULL AND p.ProductID IS NULL
            THEN 'Unknown product'
        WHEN c.CategoryID IS NULL AND p.ProductID IS NOT NULL
            THEN 'Unmapped'
        WHEN c.CategoryID IS NOT NULL
            THEN c.CategoryName
    END AS category_name,
    p.Sale_Price * od.Quantity AS line_value
FROM OrderDetails AS od
LEFT JOIN Products AS p
    ON od.ProductID = p.ProductID
FULL OUTER JOIN Category AS c
    ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID
ORDER BY od.OrderDetailID NULLS LAST;

steps.title: Why group by the category ID and its label?
steps.change: The label and category ID collect the joined rows into one group per reported category. All matched Drinks lines occupy the same group. The purple joined-row count includes rows contributed by OrderDetails, Products and Category.
steps.sql:
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN c.CategoryID IS NULL AND p.ProductID IS NULL
            THEN 'Unknown product'
        WHEN c.CategoryID IS NULL AND p.ProductID IS NOT NULL
            THEN 'Unmapped'
        WHEN c.CategoryID IS NOT NULL
            THEN c.CategoryName
    END AS category_name, COUNT(*) AS joined_rows
FROM OrderDetails AS od
LEFT JOIN Products AS p
    ON od.ProductID = p.ProductID
FULL OUTER JOIN Category AS c
    ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID
GROUP BY c.CategoryID, category_name;

steps.title: Why count orders once but add every unit?
steps.change: Count different order IDs only once per category but sum the quantity and extended list price on every line. The unmatched category has zero units. The purple value uses OrderDetails.Quantity and Products.Sale_Price.
steps.added_sql:
END AS category_name,
    COUNT(DISTINCT od.OrderID) AS orders,
    COALESCE(SUM(od.Quantity), 0) AS units_sold,
    CASE
        WHEN COUNT(od.OrderDetailID) = 0 THEN 0
        ELSE SUM(p.Sale_Price * od.Quantity)
    END AS list_price_value
steps.sql:
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN c.CategoryID IS NULL AND p.ProductID IS NULL
            THEN 'Unknown product'
        WHEN c.CategoryID IS NULL AND p.ProductID IS NOT NULL
            THEN 'Unmapped'
        WHEN c.CategoryID IS NOT NULL
            THEN c.CategoryName
    END AS category_name,
    COUNT(DISTINCT od.OrderID) AS orders,
    COALESCE(SUM(od.Quantity), 0) AS units_sold,
    CASE
        WHEN COUNT(od.OrderDetailID) = 0 THEN 0
        ELSE SUM(p.Sale_Price * od.Quantity)
    END AS list_price_value
FROM OrderDetails AS od
LEFT JOIN Products AS p
    ON od.ProductID = p.ProductID
FULL OUTER JOIN Category AS c
    ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID
GROUP BY c.CategoryID, category_name;

steps.title: Why sort by value and check the units?
steps.change: Apply the following clause to the complete learner query. Highest known value comes first. Equal values sort by category name, and unknown values come last.
steps.added_sql: ORDER BY list_price_value DESC NULLS LAST, category_name ASC;
